objective: Understand frontend versus backend plugins: what runs in the browser, what runs in Node, and how a plugin's frontend talks to its backend
secondaryObjectives: Customize Backstage plugins: installing community plugins, configuring them in app-config, and adding routes and tabs to the entity page

sources.cite: CNCF, Certified Backstage Associate (CBA) certification page: Customizing Backstage 32%, Backstage Development Workflow 24%, Backstage Infrastructure 22%, Backstage Catalog 22%
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17 (domain weights only). The objective wording is the course seed's; the cncf/curriculum PDF was not re-read (to verify).

sources.cite: Backstage documentation, Call an existing API
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: direct requests from the plugin frontend suit APIs where 'the requests do not require secrets to be passed'; 'Backstage has an optional proxy plugin for the backend, that can be used to easily add proxy routes to downstream APIs', for example to add an Authorization header; a backend plugin when you 'need to inject secrets'.

Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: the proxy config in app-config.yaml with a target and headers such as 'Authorization: Bearer ${EXAMPLE_AUTH_TOKEN}', the value interpolated from an environment variable; with the proxy mounted at /proxy, requests to /api/proxy/<path>/... go to the target; by default only safe request headers are forwarded, and allowedHeaders must list Authorization to forward the caller's.

sources.cite: Backstage documentation, Defining Configuration for your Plugin
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: the @visibility values are frontend ('Visible in frontend and backend'), backend ('(Default) Only in backend') and secret ('Only in backend and may be excluded from logs'). That frontend-visible values reach every user's browser follows from 'visible in frontend' (the page does not say 'bundle'); the PR preview's config view in the scenario is authored.

brief.situation: You maintain the Backstage developer portal at Northvale Insurance, a fictional insurer. A team installed a community frontend plugin that adds a Code quality tab to each service's entity page, reading the internal quality server's API. The tab shows 'Failed to load: 401'. Pull request #88 makes it work and is waiting for your approval; the portal is demonstrated to engineering leadership at 15:00.
handover: The quality server needs a bearer token; QUALITY_TOKEN is already set in the backend's environment.
PR #88 has been deployed to a preview environment since yesterday for testing.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the browser, the Backstage backend and its proxy, and the quality server.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: why the tab got a 401, why PR #88 is the wrong fix, and what you did instead.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Places the plugin's code in the browser and the token in the backend.
parts.modelAnswer: The community plugin is a frontend plugin: its requests run in each user's browser, which has no token, so the quality server answered 401. QUALITY_TOKEN lives only in the backend's environment.

parts.label: PR #88
parts.criteria: Explains what frontend visibility does with a secret.
parts.modelAnswer: PR #88 marked the token @visibility frontend and sent it from the browser, so every portal user receives it; the preview already showed it to any signed-in user.

parts.label: Instead
parts.criteria: Routes through the backend proxy, rotates the exposed token and checks.
parts.modelAnswer: Added a /quality proxy endpoint whose Authorization header the backend fills from QUALITY_TOKEN, pointed the plugin at /api/proxy/quality, closed #88, rotated the token the preview exposed, and confirmed a 200 with no token in the frontend config before 15:00.

scoring.modelReasoning: A frontend plugin's code runs in each user's browser, so its request to the quality server carries no token and gets a 401; the token exists only in the backend's environment. PR #88 makes it work by marking the token visible to the frontend, which delivers it to every portal user, and the preview has already shown it to anyone signed in. The plugin is built to call the quality server through the Backstage backend's proxy, which adds the Authorization header from QUALITY_TOKEN on the server side. Add that endpoint, point the plugin at /api/proxy/quality, close the PR, rotate the exposed token, and check that the tab loads and the frontend config holds no secret before the demo.
